newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Ford unions plan UK strike ballot.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ford unions plan UK strike ballot.

text.p: British car workers will hold a strike ballot against Ford as soon as possible unless the U.S. motor company reverses its decision to axe 1,300 jobs, a union official said on Thursday.
"This is the most serious dispute we have seen in our industry for two decades," Transport and General Workers Union national officer Tony Woodley said.
"We are in dispute unless and until they reverse their disgraceful decision to close Halewood (plant)."
Ford announced last week it planned to axe one in three jobs at its Halewood plant in north-west England, raising fears for jobs at 20 Ford plants across Britain.

But in closed-door talks on Thursday, union chiefs failed to persuade Ford management to reinstate the jobs. The talks were set to continue on Thursday afternoon, after which Ford planned to issue a statement.

Outside the talks, Ford workers from across the country cheered and waved banners in support of industrial action, once a regular feature of the British landscape but largely stamped out during two decades of Conservative rule.
Woodley said the unions would act as quickly as possible on the ballot but the process might take five or six weeks.
"We will be moving to a ballot as soon as humanly possible," he said to rousing cheers from the crowd.
Mass meetings of Ford workers this week reaped overwhelming support for the unions' position in opposing the company's plans, he said.
The ballot paper is expected to quiz workers as to whether they favour a strike or industrial action short of a walkout.

Ford shocked its workforce last week by announcing the job losses at Halewood, which produces Escort cars for the domestic market. It is expected to concentrate production of the next Escort model in Germany or Spain.
With Halewood's future now in doubt, Ford has asked for British government aid to maintain production there after 2000.
Unions say the decision may threaten the jobs of 10,000 other workers. They believe Halewood faces closure even though the firm has raised the prospect of a new car being built there.

"The attack on Halewood is viewed as an attack on all Ford workers in Britain. There is no justification whatever for what the company's trying to do. We have a plant that is very productive, very efficient that is producing cars in a cost-effective manner," said Woodley.
"It's very important indeed that we send a very clear message to the company."
The dispute comes as Britain goes on an election footing and could prove embarrassing for the opposition Labour Party, traditionally considered the friend of the worker.

Labour is currently some 20 points ahead in the polls but the Conservative government, which must hold an election by May 22, may use the Ford dispute to awaken old fears of a nation ruled by Labour and riven by industrial disputes.
